tools.name: exec

format.definition:
start: pragma_source | plain_source
pragma_source: PRAGMA_LINE NEWLINE SOURCE
plain_source: SOURCE

PRAGMA_LINE: /[ \t]*\/\/ @exec:[^\r\n]*/
NEWLINE: /\r?\n/
SOURCE: /[\s\S]+/

tools.name: wait
tools.description:
Waits on a yielded `exec` cell and returns new output or completion.
- Use `wait` only after `exec` returns `Script running with cell ID ...`.
- `cell_id` identifies the running `exec` cell to resume.
- `yield_time_ms` controls how long to wait for more output before yielding again. Defaults to 10000 ms.
- `max_tokens` limits how much new output this wait call returns. Defaults to 10000 tokens.
- `terminate: true` stops the running cell; false or omitted waits for output.
- `wait` returns only the new output since the last yield, or the final completion or termination result for that cell.
- If the cell is still running, `wait` may yield again with the same `cell_id`.
- If the cell has already finished, `wait` returns the completed result and closes the cell.

cell_id.description: Identifier of the running exec cell.

max_tokens.description: Output token budget for this wait call. Defaults to 10000 tokens.

terminate.description: True stops the running exec cell; false or omitted waits for output.

yield_time_ms.description: Wait before yielding more output. Defaults to 10000 ms.

tools.name: request_user_input
tools.description: Request user input for one to three short questions and wait for the response. This tool is only available in Plan mode.

questions.description: Questions to show the user. Prefer 1 and do not exceed 3

header.description: Short header label shown in the UI (12 or fewer chars).

options.description: Provide 2-3 mutually exclusive choices. Put the recommended option first and suffix its label with "(Recommended)". Do not include an "Other" option in this list; the client will add a free-form "Other" option automatically.

description.description: One short sentence explaining impact/tradeoff if selected.

question.description: Single-sentence prompt shown to the user.

tools.name: request_user_input_async
tools.description: Ask the user one or more questions during ongoing work. Use this tool only to request missing information, preferences, constraints, clarification, or approval. The tool returns immediately without ending the turn or waiting for a reply; any reply arrives asynchronously as a new user message. Keep questions concise, self-contained, and easy to understand, using a level of detail appropriate to the user and task. The UI always allows a free-text answer, including when suggested options are provided. A preselected option is not submitted automatically.

questions.description: One or more self-contained questions to present together, in display order.

options.description: Suggested answers, in display order. Put the recommended answer first; the first option is preselected by default. The user can select one option or enter a free-text answer. Do not include an Other option or a free-text placeholder; the UI provides free-text input automatically. Omit options for a free-text-only question.

title.description: The complete question shown to the user, including any context needed to answer it.

tools.name: clock
tools.description: Tools for reading and waiting on time.

tools.name: sleep
tools.description: Pause execution for a specified duration. The sleep ends early when new input arrives for the active turn. Returns the elapsed wall-clock time.

duration_ms.description: How long to sleep in milliseconds. Must be between 1 and 43200000.

tools.name: collaboration
tools.description: Tools for spawning and managing sub-agents.

tools.name: followup_task
tools.description: Send a follow-up task to an existing non-root target agent and trigger a turn if it is idle. If the target is already running, deliver the task promptly at message boundaries while sampling, or after the pending tool call completes.

message.description: Message text to send to the target agent.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to send a follow-up task to (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: interrupt_agent
tools.description: Interrupt an agent's current turn, if any, and return its previous status. The agent remains available for messages and follow-up tasks.

target.description: Agent id or canonical task name to interrupt (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: list_agents
tools.description: List live agents in the current root thread tree. Optionally filter by task-path prefix.

path_prefix.description: Task-path prefix filter without a trailing slash. Omit to list all live agents.

tools.name: send_message
tools.description: Send a message to an existing agent. The message will be delivered promptly. Does not trigger a new turn.

message.description: Message text to queue on the target agent.

target.description: Relative or canonical task name to message (from spawn_agent).

tools.name: spawn_agent
tools.description:
Available model overrides (optional; inherited parent model is preferred):
- `gpt-6.1-sol`: Latest workhorse model for coding and everyday work. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6.1-terra`: GPT-6.1 Terra Codex model. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-astra`: Frontier intelligence for the most demanding work. Reasoning efforts: low (default), medium, high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-sol`: Previous generation workhorse model. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max, ultra. Service tiers: priority.
- `gpt-6-luna`: Fast and affordable model for easier tasks. Reasoning efforts: low, medium (default), high, xhigh, max. Service tiers: priority.
        Spawns an agent to work on the specified task. If your current task is `/root/task1` and you spawn_agent with task_name "task_3" the agent will have canonical task name `/root/task1/task_3`.
You are then able to refer to this agent as `task_3` or `/root/task1/task_3` interchangeably. However an agent `/root/task2/task_3` would only be able to communicate with this agent via its canonical name `/root/task1/task_3`.
The spawned agent will have the same tools as you and the ability to spawn its own subagents.

It will be able to send you and other running agents messages, and its final answer will be provided to you when it finishes.
The new agent's canonical task name will be provided to it along with the message.

Note that passing `fork_turns="none"` will not pass any surrounding context to the spawned subagent, which may cause the agent to lack the context it needs to complete its task, whereas `fork_turns="all"` will provide the subagent with all surrounding context.

fork_turns.description: Parent history to inherit. Defaults to `all`; use `none` to start without parent history. Only `all` and `none` are supported.

message.description: Initial plain-text task for the new agent.

model.description: Model override for the new agent. Omit unless an explicit override is needed.

reasoning_effort.description: Reasoning effort override for the new agent. Omit to inherit the parent effort.

task_name.description: Task name for the new agent. Use lowercase letters, digits, and underscores.

tools.name: wait_agent
tools.description: Wait for a mailbox update from any live agent, including queued messages and final-status notifications. The wait also ends early when new user input is steered into the active turn. Does not return the content; returns either a summary of which agents have updates (if any), an interruption summary for steered input, or a timeout summary if no activity arrives before the deadline.

timeout_ms.description: Timeout in milliseconds. Defaults to 30000, min 10000, max 3600000.

<permissions instructions>
Filesystem sandboxing defines which files can be read or written. `sandbox_mode` is `workspace-write`: The sandbox permits reading files, and editing files in `cwd` and `writable_roots`. Editing files in other directories requires approval. Network access is restricted.
# Escalation Requests

Commands are run outside the sandbox if they are approved by the user, or match an existing rule that allows it to run unrestricted. The command string is split into independent command segments at shell control operators, including but not limited to:

- Pipes: |
- Logical operators: &&, ||
- Command separators: ;
- Subshell boundaries: (...), $(...)

Each resulting segment is evaluated independently for sandbox restrictions and approval requirements.

Example:

git pull | tee output.txt

This is treated as two command segments:

["git", "pull"]

["tee", "output.txt"]

Commands that use more advanced shell features like redirection (>, >>, <), substitutions ($(...), ...), environment variables (FOO=bar), or wildcard patterns (*, ?) will not be evaluated against rules, to limit the scope of what an approved rule allows.

## How to request escalation

IMPORTANT: To request approval to execute a command that will require escalated privileges:

- Provide the `sandbox_permissions` parameter with the value `"require_escalated"`
- Include a short question asking the user if they want to allow the action in `justification` parameter. e.g. "Do you want to download and install dependencies for this project?"
- Optionally suggest a `prefix_rule` - this will be shown to the user with an option to persist the rule approval for future sessions.

If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with "require_escalated". ALWAYS proceed to use the `justification` parameter - do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.

## When to request escalation

While commands are running inside the sandbox, here are some scenarios that will require escalation outside the sandbox:

- You need to run a command that writes to a directory that requires it (e.g. running tests that write to /var)
- You need to run a GUI app (e.g., open/xdg-open/osascript) to open browsers or files.
- If you run a command that is important to solving the user's query, but it fails because of sandboxing or with a likely sandbox-related network error (for example DNS/host resolution, registry/index access, or dependency download failure), rerun the command with `require_escalated`. ALWAYS proceed to use the `sandbox_permissions` and `justification` parameters. do not message the user before requesting approval for the command.
- You are about to take a potentially destructive action such as an `rm` or `git reset` that the user did not explicitly ask for.
- Be judicious with escalating, but if completing the user's request requires it, you should do so - don't try and circumvent approvals by using other tools.

## prefix_rule guidance

When choosing a `prefix_rule`, request one that will allow you to fulfill similar requests from the user in the future without re-requesting escalation. It should be categorical and reasonably scoped to similar capabilities. You should rarely pass the entire command into `prefix_rule`.

### Banned prefix_rules 
Avoid requesting overly broad prefixes that the user would be ill-advised to approve. For example, do not request ["python3"], ["python", "-"], or other similar prefixes that would allow arbitrary scripting.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule argument for destructive commands like rm.
NEVER provide a prefix_rule if your command uses a heredoc or herestring. 

### Examples
Good examples of prefixes:
- ["npm", "run", "dev"]
- ["gh", "pr", "check"]
- ["cargo", "test"]
 The writable roots are `/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1`, `/tmp`.

<multi_agent_role>You are `/root`, the primary agent in a team of agents collaborating to fulfill the user's goals.

At the start of your turn, you are the active agent.
You can spawn sub-agents to handle subtasks, and those sub-agents can spawn their own sub-agents.
All agents in the team, including the agents that you can assign tasks to, are equally intelligent and capable, and have access to the same set of tools.

You can use `spawn_agent` to create a new agent, `followup_task` to give an existing agent a new task and trigger a turn, and `send_message` to pass a message to a running agent without triggering a turn.
`send_message` calls may be read by a human, so ensure they are legible. Always put proper spaces between words and/or numbers.
Child agents can also spawn their own sub-agents.
You can decide how much context you want to propagate to your sub-agents with the `fork_turns` parameter.

You will receive messages in the analysis channel in the form:
```
Message Type: MESSAGE | FINAL_ANSWER
Task name: <recipient>
Sender: <author>
Payload:
<payload text>
```
They may be addressed as to=/root

Note that collaboration tools cannot be called from inside `functions.exec`. Call `spawn_agent`, `send_message`, `followup_task`, `wait_agent`, `interrupt_agent`, and `list_agents` only as direct tool calls using the recipient shown in their tool definitions, such as `to=functions.collaboration.spawn_agent`, since they are intentionally absent from the `functions.exec` `tools.*` namespace. Available tools in `functions.exec` are explicitly described with a `tools` namespace in the developer message.

All agents share the same directory. In detail:
- All agents have access to the same container and filesystem as you.
- All agents use the same current working directory.
- As a result, edits made by one agent are immediately visible to all other agents.

When calling `wait_agent`, prefer longer waits (minutes) to avoid busy polling.

There are 4 available concurrency slots, meaning that up to 4 agents can be active at once, including you.

Full-history forks (`fork_turns` omitted or `"all"`) inherit the parent model and reasoning effort and do not accept overrides. Only set `model` or `reasoning_effort` when explicitly requested by the user, applicable `AGENTS.md` instructions, or skill instructions; when doing so, set `fork_turns` to `"none"`.</multi_agent_role>

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

| R-62 | Queue entries and supporting extraction records shall agree on the same source version. | `docs/requirements.md` § Operating context / Shared operations — “Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.” | Proposed `tests/test_acceptance.py::test_queue_extraction_consistency`: compare document identity and source version across queue and extraction records after updates, failures and interruption; command: `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_acceptance.py -k test_queue_extraction_consistency` |
| R-63 | During slow, rate-limited or unavailable model service, operators shall be able to locate affected messages, inspect pending work and resume without losing completed work. | `docs/requirements.md` § Operating context / Service interruptions and handover — “The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work.” | Proposed `tests/test_acceptance.py::test_service_interruption_recovery`: simulate slow, rate-limited and unavailable responses and inspect affected/pending records before resuming; command: `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_acceptance.py -k test_service_interruption_recovery` |
| R-64 | Response structure and completion status shall be validated before extracted data is used. | `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior — “Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data.” | Proposed `tests/test_acceptance.py::test_response_validation_before_use`: prevent malformed or incomplete responses from entering successful extraction/routing; command: `env -u API_KEY python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_acceptance.py -k test_response_validation_before_use` |

-## Open questions
+## Open Questions
+
+These questions identify unresolved meanings, missing contracts and assumptions in the five reviewed documents. They do not change the requirements above or supply answers. References to R-IDs include their proposed checks: a check may choose an interpretation that the source has not established. Explicit choices already delegated to the implementer (such as CLI versus service versus web application) are not themselves ambiguities.
+
+### Source authority and input contract
+
+1. **OQ-01 — Authority when documents differ.** Which document takes precedence if the brief, requirements, policy and schema disagree? For example, the schema permits arbitrary date strings while the policy requires YYYY-MM-DD. Should semantic policy validation supplement schema validation, and which failures become extraction errors versus clarification issues? Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` § The task; `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` date properties; R-22–R-28, R-36, R-64.
+2. **OQ-02 — Export schema and versions.** Which export properties are mandatory, what are their types and permitted values, and which `export_version` values must be supported? Are missing metadata, extra properties and unknown versions accepted? There is an extraction schema but no formal input schema. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Workload and the review day; `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format; R-03–R-05.
+3. **OQ-03 — Invalid input handling.** What record, identity and retry behavior are required for invalid UTF-8, invalid JSON, duplicate JSON keys, a non-object root, or a missing/non-string/empty `message`? Does the extraction-failure contract also cover failures before a model request can be built? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Input export format, Processing and recovery; R-04, R-44, R-47.
+4. **OQ-04 — Input bounds.** Are “up to 200 English words” and English-only messages guaranteed input constraints or validation requirements? How should longer messages, mixed languages and borderline word counts be handled? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Input export format; R-03–R-04.
+5. **OQ-05 — Filename identity.** Does “filename” mean basename including `.json`, a relative path, or an uploaded original filename? How are identical basenames in different directories, case differences, renamed files and non-JSON filenames handled? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Input export format, Extracted facts; R-06, R-34, R-49.
+6. **OQ-06 — Identifier comparison.** How is the identifier “in its filename” obtained for arbitrary future filenames, and are case, whitespace, punctuation or leading zeros normalized before comparing it with the message's request ID? What happens when a filename has no recognizable request identifier? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-08, R-33.
+
+### Meaning of extracted facts and evidence
+
+7. **OQ-07 — Request kinds.** What distinguishes `new`, `change`, `withdrawal`, `other` and unresolved `null` when the message does not explicitly name a kind? How should renewals, extensions, temporary suspensions and requests combining kinds be classified? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` `/properties/kind`; R-10, R-28.
+8. **OQ-08 — Multiple requests in one message.** How should one document containing several people, systems, permissions or distinct requests fit the single-object, scalar-field schema: one unresolved extraction, one selected request, or another behavior? Independence between messages does not define multiplicity within a message. Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` scalar properties; R-08–R-24, R-34.
+9. **OQ-09 — Field meanings.** Does `requester` mean the author, person requesting on another's behalf, or access recipient? Whose `team` and `manager` are intended, and does `request_date` mean the message date or the date of an earlier request being discussed? What qualifies as a named manager/contact? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-09, R-11–R-12, R-19.
+10. **OQ-10 — Text normalization.** Must names, team/system names and business purposes preserve source wording, or may they be trimmed, case-normalized, expanded or paraphrased? How much detail must `business_purpose` retain to count as complete and factually correct? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / accuracy.md; R-11–R-19, R-93.
+11. **OQ-11 — Explicit facts versus interpretation.** Which linguistic inferences are allowed under “Use explicit facts”? For example, may “prod,” “read-only,” “view reports” or “full control” map to the schema enums, and how are unsupported environments or permission levels represented and explained? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` environment/permission enums; R-14–R-15, R-24, R-28.
+12. **OQ-12 — Absent values versus non-values.** Are empty strings, whitespace, “unknown,” “TBD,” “N/A” and explicitly unspecified values missing facts that must become null? The schema accepts empty strings and does not define their business meaning. Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` string properties; R-24, R-27–R-28, R-39.
+13. **OQ-13 — Date interpretation.** Which absolute input formats may be normalized, and how should ambiguous numeric dates, dates without a year, timestamps/time zones and impossible calendar dates be represented? Must malformed explicit dates become null with issues, or cause response validation to fail? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` date properties; R-26–R-28, R-64.
+14. **OQ-14 — Relative and indefinite dates.** Does “A relative date stays unresolved” also apply when the message itself supplies an explicit anchor, such as “two days after 2026-10-22”? How should “immediately,” “ongoing,” “until further notice” and partly relative date ranges be represented? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-17–R-18, R-31.
+15. **OQ-15 — Temporal validity.** Beyond start_date after end_date, do past dates, dates preceding request_date, equal start/end dates or very long access periods require clarification? Are the dates inclusive, or is that outside intake's scope? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue / rule 3; R-26, R-39.
+16. **OQ-16 — Corrections.** What wording counts as “explicitly labelled as a correction”: only “correction,” or also “actually,” “instead” and “please amend”? Does “later” mean textual position, quoted-message chronology, or another ordering? How are several corrections, a retracted correction, and a correction followed by an unlabelled contradiction handled? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-29–R-30.
+17. **OQ-17 — Conflict scope.** What distinguishes a contradiction from historical context, alternatives under consideration, conditional requests or a quoted earlier message? Must every conflict trigger clarification, including one unrelated to the requested access? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Extracted facts, Review queue / rule 3; R-28–R-29, R-39.
+18. **OQ-18 — Changes beyond permission.** For a change request, should environment, system, dates, team and manager also reflect requested new values rather than existing values? Can omitted unchanged facts be taken from context within the message, and must omitted fields remain null rather than being inherited from a different document? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-27, R-32, R-34.
+19. **OQ-19 — Evidence coverage.** Must supporting_quotes substantiate every non-null fact, or only selected facts plus conflicts and override attempts? Can one full-message quote suffice, and are minimum coverage, quote length, ordering and duplicates constrained? Empty arrays and empty quote strings are schema-valid. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Input export format, Extracted facts, Review queue / rule 1; `snapshot.schema.json` `/properties/supporting_quotes`; R-20, R-25, R-29, R-35, R-37.
+20. **OQ-20 — Correction evidence.** After a correction resolves an earlier contradiction, must evidence retain both the superseded and corrected statements, and should an issue record the correction even though the fact is resolved? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-29–R-30.
+21. **OQ-21 — Issue contract.** Must each missing/unresolved field have a separate issue, or may one issue explain several fields? Are issue text, codes, field associations, ordering and duplicates constrained? Is a factually complete request required to have no issues, or may informational issues remain without triggering clarification? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Extracted facts, Review queue; `snapshot.schema.json` `/properties/issues`; R-21, R-25, R-27–R-28, R-39.
+
+### Routing and human review
+
+22. **OQ-22 — Override definition and detection.** What qualifies as an “instruction-override attempt,” as distinct from ordinary access instructions, quoted examples or a requester asking for approval? Must detection consider the original message independently of model-produced issues/quotes, and what expected cases establish adequate detection? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue / rule 1; R-37, R-76.
+23. **OQ-23 — Withdrawal details.** Should supplied non-identity withdrawal facts still be extracted, or may they be null even when present? Which absent facts must be listed in issues? Rule 2 deliberately precedes rule 3; is confirm-withdrawal intended even when a withdrawal has an identifier mismatch, conflicting ancillary facts or reversed dates, provided request_id and request_date are resolved? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue / rules 2–3; R-27, R-38–R-39.
+24. **OQ-24 — Incomplete withdrawals.** Are request_id and request_date the complete required-fact set for withdrawals that fail rule 2, so that one missing identity/date fact routes to clarify without requiring the new/change access fields? Rule 3 only explicitly lists required facts for new/change requests. Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue / rules 2–3; R-38–R-39.
+25. **OQ-25 — Routing roles versus people.** Is `owner` always the literal role label IT Service Desk, Security Review or System Owner, or must it resolve to a named person or regional team? If actual assignments are expected, where does the system-owner/region directory come from? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue; R-40–R-43.
+26. **OQ-26 — Review lifecycle boundary.** Is the application responsible only for initial routing, or also for recording human decisions, Security Review recommendations, forwarding to system owners, clarification responses and withdrawal confirmations? If later actions are supported, what states and history are required? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue; R-42–R-43.
+27. **OQ-27 — Related-document display.** Independent documents must remain separate, but should the interface link or flag documents sharing a request_id, particularly a withdrawal and its original request? Is any effect on the original queue entry expected after human confirmation? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Extracted facts, Review queue / rule 2; R-34, R-38.
+
+### Versions, reuse and shared operation
+
+28. **OQ-28 — Revision ordering.** What defines the “latest processed source” and “latest attempt” when exports arrive out of order or overlapping jobs finish in a different order from their start? May exported_at order source revisions despite being metadata, or must intake order determine which version becomes current? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Updates and follow-up; R-54, R-57, R-60.
+29. **OQ-29 — Current view during refresh.** While an updated source/settings version is pending, should the current queue retain a clearly labelled older result, replace it with pending work, or show both? Does current mean latest completed attempt or latest submitted attempt, and when must new work first become visible? Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` § The task; `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Updates and follow-up; R-02, R-55, R-57, R-61–R-63.
+30. **OQ-30 — Pending states and outputs.** What status, owner, next_action, extraction and error values represent queued, running, waiting-to-retry or interrupted work? Must such work appear in extractions.jsonl and queue.json, or may a separate recorded-state view expose it? The defined tuples cover completed extraction/routing and errors. Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit; `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Service interruptions and handover; R-44, R-61, R-63, R-90–R-91.
+31. **OQ-31 — Relevant settings.** Which changes invalidate reuse: provider/model, endpoint, prompt, schema, sampling parameters, token limits, extraction code, routing code or policy? How are their identities/version changes recorded, and must unchanged sources be rediscovered automatically after a change or explicitly selected by the operator? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Updates and follow-up, Record and review behavior; R-48, R-58–R-59.
+32. **OQ-32 — Refresh granularity.** May a routing-only policy change reuse extracted facts and reroute them, or must it call the model again? How is that distinguished from an extraction-policy change, and how are reused extraction provenance and new routing provenance represented? Source: `docs/requirements.md` § Updates and follow-up; R-58–R-59.
+33. **OQ-33 — Reusing failures and forcing retries.** Does unchanged-source/settings reuse apply to errors as well as successes? How does an explicit retry bypass reuse, and may an operator force a new attempt after success for the required failed-retry-after-success scenario? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Record and review behavior, Verification; `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-47–R-48, R-53–R-54, R-84.
+34. **OQ-34 — Returning to an earlier version.** If a source/settings combination previously processed successfully becomes current again after intervening revisions, should the prior result be reused or a new extraction created? How is this reconciled with “Changed input creates a new result”? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-48, R-50–R-51.
+35. **OQ-35 — Shared deployment boundary.** Must overlapping operators be supported on one host/shared local store, across processes, across regional machines or over a shared filesystem/service? How many simultaneous operators and workers are assumed, and is rejecting or waiting for overlapping intake acceptable? Source: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Verification; R-60, R-85–R-86.
+36. **OQ-36 — Concurrent attempt guarantees.** Must the system prevent duplicate model calls for the same document/version, or only ensure one coherent current entry? If competing attempts have different sources/settings or success/failure outcomes, which may publish, and what earlier activity must remain recorded? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Shared operations; `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-49, R-54, R-60.
+37. **OQ-37 — Consistency boundary.** Must queue and extraction reads be mutually consistent at every observable instant, including while two output files are being published and after a crash, or is consistency after a completed operation sufficient? How should readers detect or avoid mixed generations when joining by document_id alone? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Shared operations; `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / queue.json; R-62, R-90–R-91.
+38. **OQ-38 — Durability and interruption.** Which interruptions must recovery handle: graceful stop, forced process termination, host restart, failure during persistence or storage outage? At what point is a completion guaranteed durable, and may a provider call be repeated if its response was received but not recorded? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Service interruptions and handover; R-61, R-63.
+39. **OQ-39 — History contents and retention.** Does a “trustworthy record of earlier activity” require every attempt, including errors, interrupted attempts, reroutes and cache hits, or only replaced results? Must history retain original source bytes, prompts, responses, timestamps and operator identity, and for how long? What interface must expose it? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Updates and follow-up; `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-51–R-55, R-59–R-60.
+40. **OQ-40 — Separate historical storage.** Does “Store prior versions separately from current outputs” permit separate tables/records in one database, or require different files/directories? Must history be committed with the deliverables or only retained by the running application? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-52, R-90–R-91.
+
+### Provider behavior and operational limits
+
+41. **OQ-41 — Supported provider configuration.** Which provider, endpoint and model are available through API_KEY, and is any particular provider compatibility required? Which settings must operators be able to configure versus those the implementation may fix and document? Source: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; R-69–R-70, R-87, R-97.
+42. **OQ-42 — Completion and content validation.** What constitutes a valid completed response for the supported provider, including missing completion markers, multiple output candidates, refusal accompanying JSON, tool calls, fenced JSON or extra prose? May the application repair malformed output or retry it before recording failure, and must such repairs remain visible? Source: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; R-64–R-68.
+43. **OQ-43 — Semantic extraction failures.** If a response passes the schema but invents a quote, omits a required explanatory issue or contains facts unsupported by the message, must runtime validation reject it, convert fields to null/clarification, or leave detection to accuracy verification? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Extracted facts, Processing and recovery; R-22, R-27–R-29, R-35, R-44.
+44. **OQ-44 — Retry and timeout policy.** What timeouts, retryable error classes, retry count, backoff and rate-limit behavior are expected? Is a rate-limited/temporarily unavailable response immediately a current error or pending automatic retry, and is retry per document, per attempt or per batch? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Service interruptions and handover; `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-44, R-47, R-63, R-66.
+45. **OQ-45 — Retry reproducibility.** Must a retry command reproduce the failed attempt's source bytes/settings/policy, or process the latest available source/configuration? What happens if the original file has changed or disappeared? Source: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; R-47, R-55, R-59.
+46. **OQ-46 — Workload acceptance criteria.** Are 200–400 daily messages and roughly 2,000-message intakes sizing context or mandatory tested capacities? What time, memory, concurrency and cost bounds define acceptable behavior, and how quickly must completed work become inspectable while another response is slow? Source: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Workload and the review day, Verification; R-45–R-46, R-85–R-86.
+47. **OQ-47 — Actionable errors and redaction.** What minimum error details make a failure actionable: category, provider code, attempt ID, retry command or all of these? Must redaction cover headers, exception bodies, URLs and persisted request/response evidence as well as logs, and what sensitive values count as credentials? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / request-evidence.json; R-44, R-47, R-71–R-72, R-94.
+
+### Deliverable contracts and verification
+
+48. **OQ-48 — Wrapper and queue formats.** Beyond the listed fields, what are the exact JSON types and allowed extra properties for extraction wrappers and queue.json? Is the queue a list or keyed object, which fields must it carry, and are ordering and hash representation prescribed? The supplied schema only defines the extraction object. Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / extractions.jsonl, queue.json; `snapshot.schema.json`; R-07, R-90–R-91.
+49. **OQ-49 — Response provenance on failure.** What response_source identifies a timeout, transport error, invalid input or refusal when no model produced a valid record? For provider successes, what syntax distinguishes provider and model IDs, and should a configured model alias or returned resolved model ID be recorded? Source: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / extractions.jsonl; R-44, R-90.
+50. **OQ-50 — Submitted record population.** Must the committed extraction/queue outputs contain exactly the 20 supplied messages, or also the authored paraphrase and any additional processed documents? Must every sample have a successful extraction, or are accurately labelled error records acceptable in the final outputs? Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` §§ The task, What to submit, Submission; R-80, R-90–R-92.
+51. **OQ-51 — Accuracy fields and denominator.** Must comparison cover all 14 schema fields, selected scalar facts, routing fields, or a combination? How are nulls, error records, absent outputs, extra records and repeated runs counted, and is accuracy aggregated per field or per document? The brief asks for rules but does not prescribe one scoring contract. Source: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / accuracy.md; R-92–R-93.
+52. **OQ-52 — Exact match and factual errors.** Does exact match allow any normalization for text or order-insensitive arrays? How should semantically equivalent business-purpose wording, different valid quotes or issue explanations be scored? What distinguishes a factual error from a formatting, evidence or routing error? Source: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / accuracy.md; R-16, R-20–R-21, R-81, R-93.
+53. **OQ-53 — Accuracy acceptance threshold.** Is a minimum extraction/routing accuracy or maximum factual-error rate required, or is a reproducible source-grounded report sufficient regardless of score? How should remaining known errors affect submission acceptance? Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` §§ What to submit, Submission; `docs/requirements.md` § Verification; R-81, R-93, R-97.
+54. **OQ-54 — Mock evidence versus extraction validation.** Since live observations are optional, what must the accuracy check demonstrate when measured outputs are mocked: comparison mechanics only, or behavior of the implemented extractor? How are mocks to be constructed independently enough that matching their authored expectations is not presented as model accuracy? Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` § Submission; `docs/requirements.md` § Verification; R-81, R-93, R-97–R-99.
+55. **OQ-55 — Paraphrase contract.** Must the authored paraphrase preserve all facts of one supplied message, or may it be a new synthetic scenario? Must its expected quotes/issues and routing be specified, and must it run through the same ingestion/provider path as the supplied messages? Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / accuracy.md; `docs/requirements.md` § Verification; R-80, R-92.
+56. **OQ-56 — Required test scope.** Does “checks for refusal or interrupted responses” require both cases or either one? R-82 and R-83 choose both, while the broader behavior requirement explicitly names both. Which operational scenarios must be automated rather than documented/manual, given “situations your design handles”? Source: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Record and review behavior, Verification; R-67–R-68, R-82–R-86.
+57. **OQ-57 — Proposed tests versus source requirements.** Are sample-specific facts and test assumptions in the spec independently verified expectations or still proposals? For example, R-48's check requires no model request on reuse, R-81's check says “manually specified” although the source says independently specified, and R-90's check targets all 20 filenames without resolving additional-document scope. Should these interpretations become requirements or be revised after clarification? Sources: `planning/spec.md` introduction and cited checks; `docs/requirements.md` §§ Record and review behavior, Verification; `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit.
+58. **OQ-58 — Test runner portability.** If the implementation uses another runtime/interface, must the proposed Python unittest commands still invoke acceptance tests, or may equivalent checks replace them? The introduction disclaims a prescribed language but also describes an existing unittest runner. Source: `planning/spec.md` introduction and proposed test commands; R-02, R-87.
+59. **OQ-59 — Request evidence detail.** Does request-evidence.json need an actual captured request or may it contain a representative constructed example? Must it include the full prompt/schema and example responses for each handling branch, or is a description/reference to implemented response handling sufficient? How should several supported configurations be represented? Source: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / request-evidence.json; R-94.
+60. **OQ-60 — Observation labels.** Does “each recorded observation” require configuration and mock/provider labels on every assertion/result, or may one labelled run/header cover several observations? How should non-model observations such as concurrency, persistence and lockfile checks be labelled? Source: `CHALLENGE.md` § Submission; R-95, R-99.
+61. **OQ-61 — Lockfile without dependencies.** If the implementation uses only its runtime's standard library, what artifact satisfies the unconditional “dependency lockfile” submission item? Source: `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / Source code and dependency lockfile; R-89.
+62. **OQ-62 — Facilitator-controlled submission details.** Which capture artifact/format and commit-pairing procedure are required, and how is the capture included or linked in the submission? The referenced facilitator capture and Classroom assignment instructions are not defined in these five documents. Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` §§ What to submit / Coding-session capture, Submission; R-96, R-100–R-101.
*** End Patch"));

Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-09, R-11–R-12, R-19.

How much detail must `business_purpose` retain to count as complete and factually correct? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `CHALLENGE.md` § What to submit / accuracy.md; R-11–R-19, R-93.

For example, may “prod,” “read-only,” “view reports” or “full control” map to the schema enums, and how are unsupported environments or permission levels represented and explained? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` environment/permission enums; R-14–R-15, R-24, R-28.
+12. **OQ-12 — Absent values versus non-values.** Are empty strings, whitespace, “unknown,” “TBD,” “N/A” and explicitly unspecified values missing facts that must become null? Must malformed explicit dates become null with issues, or cause response validation to fail? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; `snapshot.schema.json` date properties; R-26–R-28, R-64.
+14. **OQ-14 — Relative and indefinite dates.** Does “A relative date stays unresolved” also apply when the message itself supplies an explicit anchor, such as “two days after 2026-10-22”? How should “immediately,” “ongoing,” “until further notice” and partly relative date ranges be represented? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-17–R-18, R-31.

Are the dates inclusive, or is that outside intake's scope? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue / rule 3; R-26, R-39.
+16. **OQ-16 — Corrections.** What wording counts as “explicitly labelled as a correction”: only “correction,” or also “actually,” “instead” and “please amend”? Does “later” mean textual position, quoted-message chronology, or another ordering? How are several corrections, a retracted correction, and a correction followed by an unlabelled contradiction handled? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-29–R-30.
+17. **OQ-17 — Conflict scope.** What distinguishes a contradiction from historical context, alternatives under consideration, conditional requests or a quoted earlier message? Must every conflict trigger clarification, including one unrelated to the requested access? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Extracted facts, Review queue / rule 3; R-28–R-29, R-39.
+18. **OQ-18 — Changes beyond permission.** For a change request, should environment, system, dates, team and manager also reflect requested new values rather than existing values? Can omitted unchanged facts be taken from context within the message, and must omitted fields remain null rather than being inherited from a different document? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-27, R-32, R-34.
+19. **OQ-19 — Evidence coverage.** Must supporting_quotes substantiate every non-null fact, or only selected facts plus conflicts and override attempts? Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Input export format, Extracted facts, Review queue / rule 1; `snapshot.schema.json` `/properties/supporting_quotes`; R-20, R-25, R-29, R-35, R-37.
+20. **OQ-20 — Correction evidence.** After a correction resolves an earlier contradiction, must evidence retain both the superseded and corrected statements, and should an issue record the correction even though the fact is resolved? Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Extracted facts; R-29–R-30.
+21. **OQ-21 — Issue contract.** Must each missing/unresolved field have a separate issue, or may one issue explain several fields? Are issue text, codes, field associations, ordering and duplicates constrained? Is a factually complete request required to have no issues, or may informational issues remain without triggering clarification? Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Extracted facts, Review queue; `snapshot.schema.json` `/properties/issues`; R-21, R-25, R-27–R-28, R-39.
