# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check that this computer and this copy of the repository are ready for the Challenge.

Run it from the root of your clone:

    python3 tools/check_prerequisites.py

It checks four things and prints PASS or FAIL for each, with what to do on a FAIL:

  1. Codex is installed and signed in.
  2. This folder is a clone of the Challenge repository, with every supplied file in place.
  3. Entire records your coding sessions in this repository.
  4. The repository's tests run on mock responses: no model is called and API_KEY is not used.

The last line is READY when all four pass. Python 3.10 or later, standard library only.
"""
from __future__ import annotations

import json
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
SUPPLIED = ["CHALLENGE.md", "snapshot.schema.json", "materials/office-policy.md", "docs/requirements.md"]
REQUESTS = 20


def run(command: list[str], env: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess:
    return subprocess.run(command, cwd=ROOT, env=env, capture_output=True, text=True, timeout=300,
                          stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL)


def check_codex() -> tuple[bool, str]:
    if not shutil.which("codex"):
        return False, "codex is not on your PATH. Install the Codex CLI the way the facilitator shows you, then open a new terminal."
    version = run(["codex", "--version"])
    if version.returncode != 0:
        return False, f"codex --version failed: {version.stderr.strip() or version.stdout.strip()}"
    login = run(["codex", "login", "status"])
    if login.returncode != 0:
        return False, f"{version.stdout.strip()} is installed but not signed in. Sign in with the class key the facilitator gives you."
    return True, f"{version.stdout.strip()}; {login.stdout.strip() or login.stderr.strip()}"


def check_clone() -> tuple[bool, str]:
    inside = run(["git", "rev-parse", "--show-toplevel"])
    if inside.returncode != 0 or Path(inside.stdout.strip()).resolve() != ROOT:
        return False, "this folder is not the top of a Git clone. Clone your copy of the repository and run this from its root."
    if not run(["git", "remote", "get-url", "origin"]).stdout.strip():
        return False, "the clone has no remote named origin. Clone your copy of the repository from GitHub."
    missing = [name for name in SUPPLIED if not (ROOT / name).is_file()]
    if missing:
        return False, f"missing supplied files: {', '.join(missing)}. Clone the repository again."
    exports = sorted((ROOT / "materials" / "requests").glob("*.json"))
    if len(exports) != REQUESTS:
        return False, f"materials/requests/ holds {len(exports)} JSON files, not {REQUESTS}. Clone the repository again."
    for path in exports:
        try:
            if not isinstance(json.loads(path.read_bytes().decode("utf-8")).get("message"), str):
                return False, f"{path.name} has no message text. Clone the repository again."
        except (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError, AttributeError):
            return False, f"{path.name} is not UTF-8 JSON. Clone the repository again."
    return True, f"clone of {run(['git', 'remote', 'get-url', 'origin']).stdout.strip()}; {len(exports)} request exports read"


def check_capture() -> tuple[bool, str]:
    if not shutil.which("entire"):
        return False, "entire is not on your PATH. Install the Entire CLI as the course's session-capture guide says."
    status = run(["entire", "status", "--json"])
    try:
        state = json.loads(status.stdout)
    except ValueError:
        return False, f"entire status gave no answer: {status.stderr.strip() or status.stdout.strip()}"
    if not state.get("enabled"):
        return False, "Entire is not enabled in this repository. Run: entire enable --agent codex"
    if "Codex" not in (state.get("agents") or []):
        return False, "Entire is enabled but not for Codex. Run: entire agent add codex"
    return True, f"Entire enabled for {', '.join(state['agents'])}"


def check_tests() -> tuple[bool, str]:
    env = {key: value for key, value in os.environ.items() if key != "API_KEY"}
    tests = run([sys.executable, "-m", "unittest", "discover", "-s", "tests"], env=env)
    summary = [line for line in tests.stderr.splitlines() if line.startswith(("Ran ", "OK", "FAILED"))]
    if tests.returncode != 0:
        return False, "the tests failed with API_KEY unset:\n" + tests.stderr.strip()
    return True, "; ".join(summary) + " (API_KEY unset)"

    if sys.version_info < (3, 10):
        print(f"FAIL  Python {sys.version.split()[0]}: this Challenge needs Python 3.10 or later.")
        return 1
    checks = [("Codex", check_codex), ("Repository", check_clone),

# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

L89: ## Regular Expressions
L90: 
L91: The `pattern` keyword is used to restrict a string to a particular regular expression. The regular expression syntax is the one defined in JavaScript (【7†ECMA 262†www.ecma-international.org】 specifically) with Unicode support. See 【8†Regular Expressions】 for more information.
L92: When defining the regular expressions, it's important to note that the string is considered valid if the expression matches anywhere within the string. For example, the regular expression `"p"` will match any string with a `p` in it, such as `"apple"` not just a string that is simply `"p"`. Therefore, it is usually less confusing, as a matter of course, to surround the regular expression in `^...$`, for example, `"^p$"`, unless there is a good reason not to do so.

L113: ## Pattern Properties
L114: 
L115: Sometimes you want to say that, given a particular kind of property name, the value should match a particular schema. That's where `patternProperties` comes in: it maps regular expressions to schemas. If a property name matches the given regular expression, the property value must validate against the corresponding schema.
L116: Regular expressions are not anchored. This means that when defining the regular expressions for `patternProperties`, it's important to note that the expression may match anywhere within the property name. For example, the regular expression `"p"` will match any property name with a `p` in it, such as `"apple"`, not just a property whose name is simply `"p"`. It's therefore usually less confusing to surround the regular expression in `^...$`, for example, `"^p$"`.
L117: In this example, any properties whose names start with the prefix `S_` must be strings, and any with the prefix `I_` must be integers. Any properties that do not match either regular expression are ignored.

L77: 
L78:     Abstract
L79: 
L80:        JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) is a lightweight, text-based,
L81:        language-independent data interchange format.  It was derived from
L82:        the ECMAScript Programming Language Standard.  JSON defines a small
L83:        set of formatting rules for the portable representation of structured
L84:        data.

L86:        This document removes inconsistencies with other specifications of
L87:        JSON, repairs specification errors, and offers experience-based
L88:        interoperability guidance.

L5: * * *
L6: This module provides a portable way of using operating system dependent functionality. If you just want to read or write a file see 【2†`open()`】, if you want to manipulate paths, see the 【3†`os.path`】 module, and if you want to read all the lines in all the files on the command line see the 【4†`fileinput`】 module. L7: Notes on the availability of these functions:
L8: 
L9:   * The design of all built-in operating system dependent modules of Python is such that as long as the same functionality is available, it uses the same interface; for example, the function `os.stat(path)` returns stat information about path in the same format (which happens to have originated with the POSIX interface).
L10:   * Extensions peculiar to a particular operating system are also available through the `os` module, but using them is of course a threat to portability.
L11: 
L12:   * All functions accepting path or file names accept both bytes and string objects, and result in an object of the same type, if a path or file name is returned.
L13: 
L14:   * On VxWorks, os.popen, os.fork, os.execv and os.spawn*p* are not supported.
L15:   * On WebAssembly platforms, Android and iOS, large parts of the `os` module are not available or behave differently. APIs related to processes (e.g. 【7†`fork()`】, 【8†`execve()`】) and resources (e.g. 【9†`nice()`】) are not available. Others like 【10†`getuid()`】 and 【11†`getpid()`】 are emulated or stubs. L34: ## File Names, Command Line Arguments, and Environment Variables【20†¶】
L35: 
L36: In Python, file names, command line arguments, and environment variables are represented using the string type. On some systems, decoding these strings to and from bytes is necessary before passing them to the operating system. Python uses the 【21†filesystem encoding and error handler】 to perform this conversion (see 【22†`sys.getfilesystemencoding()`】).
L37: The 【21†filesystem encoding and error handler】 are configured at Python startup by the 【23†`PyConfig_Read()`】 function: see 【24†`filesystem_encoding`】 and 【25†`filesystem_errors`】 members of 【26†`PyConfig`】.

L39: The 【21†file system encoding】 must guarantee to successfully decode all bytes below 128. If the file system encoding fails to provide this guarantee, API functions can raise 【28†`UnicodeError`】.

L48: The Python UTF-8 Mode ignores the 【29†locale encoding】 and forces the usage of the UTF-8 encoding:

L55:   * 【36†`sys.stdin`】, 【37†`sys.stdout`】, and 【38†`sys.stderr`】 all use UTF-8 as their text encoding, with the `surrogateescape` 【39†error handler】 being enabled for `sys.stdin` and `sys.stdout` (`sys.stderr` continues to use `backslashreplace` as it does in the default locale-aware mode)

L2: 
L3: Source code: 【1†Lib/hashlib.py†github.com】
L4: 
L5: * * *
L6: This module implements a common interface to many different hash algorithms. Included are the FIPS secure hash algorithms SHA224, SHA256, SHA384, SHA512, (defined in 【2†the FIPS 180-4 standard†csrc.nist.gov】), the SHA-3 series (defined in 【3†the FIPS 202 standard†csrc.nist.gov】) as well as the legacy algorithms SHA1 (【4†formerly part of FIPS†csrc.nist.gov】) and the MD5 algorithm (defined in internet 【5†RFC 1321†datatracker.ietf.org】).
L7: 
L8: Note
L9: If you want the adler32 or crc32 hash functions, they are available in the 【6†`zlib`】 module.
L10: ## Hash algorithms【7†¶】
L11: 
L12: There is one constructor method named for each type of hash. All return a hash object with the same simple interface. For example: use 【8†`sha256()`】 to create a SHA-256 hash object. You can now feed this object with 【9†bytes-like objects】 (normally 【10†`bytes`】) using the 【11†`update`】 method. At any point you can ask it for the digest of the concatenation of the data fed to it so far using the 【12†`digest()`】 or 【13†`hexdigest()`】 methods.
L13: To allow multithreading, the Python 【14†GIL】 is released while computing a hash supplied more than 2047 bytes of data at once in its constructor or 【11†`.update`】 method.
L14: Constructors for hash algorithms that are always present in this module are 【15†`md5()`】, 【16†`sha1()`】, 【17†`sha224()`】, 【8†`sha256()`】, 【18†`sha384()`】, 【19†`sha512()`】, 【20†`sha3_224()`】, 【21†`sha3_256()`】, 【22†`sha3_384()`】, 【23†`sha3_512()`】, 【24†`shake_128()`】, 【25†`shake_256()`】, 【26†`blake2b()`】, and 【27†`blake2s()`】. These correspond to 【28†`algorithms_guaranteed`】.
L15: Any of these may nonetheless be missing or blocked in unusual environments, such as a rare “FIPS compliant” build of Python or when OpenSSL’s “FIPS mode” is configured to exclude some algorithms from its default provider. Calling the constructor of an algorithm that is unavailable raises 【29†`ValueError`】.
L16: Additional algorithms may also be available if your Python distribution’s `hashlib` was linked against a build of OpenSSL that provides others. Others are not guaranteed available on all installations and will only be accessible by name via 【30†`new()`】. See 【31†`algorithms_available`】.
L17: 
L18: Warning
L19: Some algorithms have known hash collision weaknesses (including MD5 and SHA1). Refer to 【32†Attacks on cryptographic hash algorithms†en.wikipedia.org】 and the 【33†hashlib-seealso】 section at the end of this document.
L20: 
L21: Added in version 3.6: SHA3 (Keccak) and SHAKE constructors 【20†`sha3_224()`】, 【21†`sha3_256()`】, 【22†`sha3_384()`】, 【23†`sha3_512()`】, 【24†`shake_128()`】, 【25†`shake_256()`】 were added. 【26†`blake2b()`】 and 【27†`blake2s()`】 were added.
L22: Changed in version 3.9: All hashlib constructors take a keyword-only argument usedforsecurity with default value `True`. A false value allows the use of insecure and blocked hashing algorithms in restricted environments. `False` indicates that the hashing algorithm is not used in a security context, e.g. as a non-cryptographic one-way compression function.
L23: 
L24: Changed in version 3.9: Hashlib now uses SHA3 and SHAKE from OpenSSL if it provides it.
L25: Changed in version 3.12: For any of the MD5, SHA1, SHA2, or SHA3 algorithms that the linked OpenSSL does not provide we fall back to a verified implementation from the 【34†HACL* project†github.com】.

L27: Deprecated since version 3.15, will be removed in version 3.19: The undocumented `string` keyword parameter in `_hashlib.new()` and hash-named constructors such as `_md5.md5()` is deprecated. Prefer passing the initial data as a positional argument for maximum backwards compatibility.
L28: ## Usage【35†¶】
L29: 
L30: To obtain the digest of the byte string `b"Nobody inspects the spammish repetition"`:
L31: 
L32:     >>> import hashlib
L33:     >>> m = hashlib.sha256()
L34:     >>> m.update(b"Nobody inspects")
L35:     >>> m.update(b" the spammish repetition")
L36:     >>> m.digest()
L37:     b'\x03\x1e\xdd}Ae\x15\x93\xc5\xfe\\\x00o\xa5u+7\xfd\xdf\xf7\xbcN\x84:\xa6\xaf\x0c\x95\x0fK\x94\x06'
L38:     >>> m.hexdigest()

L40: More condensed:
L41: 
L42:     >>> hashlib.sha256(b"Nobody inspects the spammish repetition").hexdigest()
L43:     '031edd7d41651593c5fe5c006fa5752b37fddff7bc4e843aa6af0c950f4b9406'
L44: ## Constructors【36†¶】
L45: 
L46: hashlib.new(name, [data, ]*, usedforsecurity=True)【30†¶】

L48: 
L49: Is a generic constructor that takes the string name of the desired algorithm as its first parameter. It also exists to allow access to the above listed hashes as well as any other algorithms that your OpenSSL library may offer.

L356: ## Standard Compliance and Interoperability【58†¶】
L357: 
L359: This module does not comply with the RFC in a strict fashion, implementing some extensions that are valid JavaScript but not valid JSON. In particular:
L360: 
L361:   * Infinite and NaN number values are accepted and output;
L362: 
L363:   * Repeated names within an object are accepted, and only the value of the last name-value pair is used.
L364: 
L365: Since the RFC permits RFC-compliant parsers to accept input texts that are not RFC-compliant, this module’s deserializer is technically RFC-compliant under default settings.
L366: ### Character Encodings【59†¶】
L367: 
L368: The RFC requires that JSON be represented using either UTF-8, UTF-16, or UTF-32, with UTF-8 being the recommended default for maximum interoperability.
L369: 
L370: As permitted, though not required, by the RFC, this module’s serializer sets ensure_ascii=True by default, thus escaping the output so that the resulting strings only contain printable ASCII characters.
L371: Other than the ensure_ascii parameter, this module is defined strictly in terms of conversion between Python objects and 【18†`Unicode strings`】, and thus does not otherwise directly address the issue of character encodings.
L372: The RFC prohibits adding a byte order mark (BOM) to the start of a JSON text, and this module’s serializer does not add a BOM to its output. The RFC permits, but does not require, JSON deserializers to ignore an initial BOM in their input. This module’s deserializer raises a 【25†`ValueError`】 when an initial BOM is present.
L373: The RFC does not explicitly forbid JSON strings which contain byte sequences that don’t correspond to valid Unicode characters (e.g. unpaired UTF-16 surrogates), but it does note that they may cause interoperability problems. By default, this module accepts and outputs (when present in the original 【18†`str`】) code points for such sequences.
L374: ### Infinite and NaN Number Values【60†¶】
L375: The RFC does not permit the representation of infinite or NaN number values. Despite that, by default, this module accepts and outputs `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, and `NaN` as if they were valid JSON number literal values:
L376: 
L377:     >>> # Neither of these calls raises an exception, but the results are not valid JSON
L378:     >>> json.dumps(float('-inf'))
L379:     '-Infinity'
L380:     >>> json.dumps(float('nan'))
L381:     'NaN'
L382:     >>> # Same when deserializing
L383:     >>> json.loads('-Infinity')
L384:     -inf
L385:     >>> json.loads('NaN')
L386:     nan
L387: In the serializer, the allow_nan parameter can be used to alter this behavior. In the deserializer, the parse_constant parameter can be used to alter this behavior.
L388: ### Repeated Names Within an Object【61†¶】
L389: 
L390: The RFC specifies that the names within a JSON object should be unique, but does not mandate how repeated names in JSON objects should be handled. By default, this module does not raise an exception; instead, it ignores all but the last name-value pair for a given name:
L391: 
L392:     >>> weird_json = '{"x": 1, "x": 2, "x": 3}'
L393:     >>> json.loads(weird_json)
L394:     {'x': 3}
L395: 
L396: 
L397: The object_pairs_hook parameter can be used to alter this behavior.
L398: ### Top-level Non-Object, Non-Array Values【62†¶】
L399: 
L400: The old version of JSON specified by the obsolete 【4†RFC 4627†datatracker.ietf.org】 required that the top-level value of a JSON text must be either a JSON object or array (Python 【37†`dict`】 or 【39†`list`】), and could not be a JSON null, boolean, number, or string value. 【3†RFC 7159†datatracker.ietf.org】 removed that restriction, and this module does not and has never implemented that restriction in either its serializer or its deserializer.
L401: Regardless, for maximum interoperability, you may wish to voluntarily adhere to the restriction yourself.
L402: ### Implementation Limitations【63†¶】
L403: 
L404: Some JSON deserializer implementations may set limits on:
L405: 
L406:   * the size of accepted JSON texts
L407: 
L408:   * the maximum level of nesting of JSON objects and arrays
L409: 
L410:   * the range and precision of JSON numbers
L411: 
L412:   * the content and maximum length of JSON strings
L413: 
L414: This module does not impose any such limits beyond those of the relevant Python datatypes themselves or the Python interpreter itself.

I left `spec.md` unchanged. The repository contains starter checks and examples, but no pipeline implementation, selected storage system, or provider integration. That limits what tool documentation can resolve.

1. **OQ-01 — Which revision wins?**

   **Files first:** [requirements.md — Updates and follow-up](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:19), [office-policy.md — Processing and recovery](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:28), and the exports in `materials/requests/`.

   **Found:** The current view must reflect the latest processed source. A later failed attempt must appear as the current error, with earlier results retained. All 20 supplied exports have the same export timestamp, so the examples do not establish revision ordering.

   **Tool/standard documentation:** Python’s [hashlib documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html) explains hashing bytes. A digest identifies content; it supplies no chronological ordering.

   **Still open:** Whether intake order, export time or another sequence determines the winner, especially when attempts finish out of order.

2. **OQ-02 — What concurrency must be supported?**

   **Files first:** [requirements.md — Shared operations](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:13) and [Verification](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:41).

   **Found:** Overlapping operators sharing records are explicitly expected. They must leave a coherent current queue and trustworthy history. The implementation must document its shared-operation assumptions.

   **Tool/standard documentation:** No database, locking mechanism or deployment platform is selected. There is consequently no named tool whose documentation establishes the concurrency guarantees.

   **Still open:** Whether support must span processes or machines, whether overlapping intake may wait or be rejected, and whether duplicate provider calls must be prevented.

3. **OQ-03 — When are results durable and mutually consistent?**

   **Files first:** [requirements.md — Shared operations](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:13), [office-policy.md — Processing and recovery](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:28), and `CHALLENGE.md`’s extraction/queue deliverables.

   **Found:** Recovery must distinguish finished from unfinished work, preserve completed work, and keep queue and extraction records on the same source version. No persistence implementation exists.

   **Tool documentation:** Python documents atomic replacement of an individual file through [`os.replace`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.replace) and flushing file data through [`os.fsync`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/os.html#os.fsync). Those primitives alone do **not** establish a transaction spanning queue and extraction files; that is an implementation inference.

   **Still open:** The crash scenarios covered, the durable completion point, and how publication and recovery prevent mixed output versions.

4. **OQ-04 — How are outages bounded and retries controlled?**

   **Files first:** [requirements.md — Service interruptions](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:27), [Record and review behavior](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:33), and [office-policy.md — Processing and recovery](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:28).

   **Found:** Failures need a reproducible retry command; unaffected messages must continue. Failed retries must retain prior successes in history. The `timeout=300` in `tools/check_prerequisites.py` applies to setup-check subprocesses—it is not a model timeout.

   **Tool documentation:** No provider or SDK is selected. Its timeout defaults, automatic retries and rate-limit handling therefore cannot yet be checked against official documentation.

   **Still open:** Retry limits/backoff, whether errors are cached, and whether retry reproduces the failed source/settings or uses current ones.

5. **OQ-05 — What changes invalidate cached results?**

   **Files first:** [requirements.md — Updates and follow-up](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:19), its [reuse requirement](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:38), and `snapshot.schema.json`.

   **Found:** Unchanged source and relevant settings require reuse. Changes affecting extraction or routing require refresh, with settings and policy provenance available. The files do not enumerate all relevant settings.

   **Tool/standard documentation:** [hashlib](https://docs.python.org/3/library/hashlib.html) provides digest computation, but does not define what an application must include in a cache key.

   **Still open:** Whether prompt/schema/code changes invalidate results, whether routing-only changes need another model call, and how affected documents are selected for refresh.

6. **OQ-06 — What constitutes a valid, uniquely identified input?**

   **Files first:** [office-policy.md — Input export format](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:5), [starter input test](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/tests/test_starter.py:28), `tools/check_prerequisites.py`, and `materials/requests/IT-001.json`.

   **Found:** Inputs are UTF-8 JSON with a `message` string; identity comes from filename and hashing uses original bytes. All examples use export version `1.0`. Starter checks verify sample readability, but do not define production error records or filename collision handling.

   **Tool/standard documentation:** [`Path.name`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/pathlib.html#pathlib.PurePath.name) means the final path component. [RFC 8259 §4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259#section-4) recommends unique object keys; Python’s [`json` decoder](https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html#repeated-names-within-an-object) accepts duplicates by default and keeps the last value.

   **Still open:** Identity across directories, supported export versions, strictness of parsing, and how malformed inputs become visible per-document failures.

7. **OQ-07 — What do operators see while work is pending?**

   **Files first:** `CHALLENGE.md` § The task, [requirements.md — Shared operations](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:13), and [office-policy.md — Processing and recovery](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:28).

   **Found:** Completed results must remain inspectable while other requests are pending. Operators must distinguish unfinished work and resume it. After a later attempt fails, its error must be current. The files define completed routing/error states, but no pending-state contract.

   **Tool/standard documentation:** JSON defines representation, not application lifecycle states. No queue engine or workflow tool is named.

   **Still open:** Whether an older result remains visible during refresh, how it is labelled, and where queued/running/retrying/interrupted states appear.

8. **OQ-08 — What validation blocks publication?**

   **Files first:** [snapshot.schema.json](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/snapshot.schema.json), [requirements.md — Response validation](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:35), and [office-policy.md — Extracted facts](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:10).

   **Found:** Structure and completion status must be checked before use. Quotes must match decoded message substrings; uncertain facts become null with issues. The schema has no date-format or minimum-length constraints, and cannot establish whether facts are source-supported.

   **Standard documentation:** JSON Schema’s [string documentation](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/string) confirms empty strings satisfy `type: string`. Its [object documentation](https://json-schema.org/understanding-json-schema/reference/object#required) explains that `required` concerns property presence, rather than business completeness.

   **Still open:** Which semantic checks run automatically, which violations cause extraction errors versus clarification, and whether automatic repair is permitted. The need for validation beyond the schema is already established.

9. **OQ-09 — What reliably triggers instruction-override review?**

   **Files first:** [office-policy.md — Rule 1](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/office-policy.md:20), [IT-006.json](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/materials/requests/IT-006.json), and [requirements.md — Verification](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:41).

   **Found:** IT-006 supplies a clear example: instructions to bypass review, reveal credentials and mark the request approved. Policy requires service-desk inspection, supporting evidence and an issue. Approval remains a human decision.

   **Tool/standard documentation:** No detection tool or model provider is selected. JSON/schema documentation cannot determine whether prose constitutes an override attempt.

   **Still open:** Detection criteria beyond the obvious example, treatment of harmless quoted instructions, and whether routing checks the original message independently of model output.

10. **OQ-10 — What service level must the pipeline sustain?**

    **Files first:** [requirements.md — Workload](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:7), [Verification](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/docs/requirements.md:41), and [starter tests](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests-1/tests/test_starter.py:27).

    **Found:** The context specifies 200–400 messages daily and surges around 2,000. Slow responses must leave other work available. Documentation must state operating assumptions and verification limits. Starter tests cover 20 inputs and a canned response; they provide no capacity evidence.

    **Tool documentation:** No provider/model/account quota is specified, so official rate-limit documentation cannot establish available throughput.

    **Still open:** A measurable completion-time target, resource/cost limits, supported surge capacity and acceptable delay before completed results become visible.

## Open Questions

These are the 10 highest-impact unresolved decisions for a production pipeline, prioritized by the risk of lost work, stale or inconsistent records, blocked recovery and incorrect routing. Related questions are consolidated; the requirements above remain unchanged.

1. **OQ-01 — Which revision wins?** When exports arrive out of order or concurrent attempts finish in reverse order, does “latest” mean export time, intake order or completion order? What prevents an older attempt from replacing a newer source or its error?

   **Production impact:** Reviewers could act on obsolete access details while the queue appears current. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Updates and follow-up; R-54, R-57, R-60.

2. **OQ-02 — What concurrency must be supported?** Are overlapping operators on one host, separate processes or separate regional machines? Must duplicate processing be prevented, or only duplicate publication, and may overlapping intake wait or be rejected?

   **Production impact:** An unsuitable coordination mechanism could cause lost updates, duplicate provider calls or corrupted history. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Shared operations; `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-49, R-60.

3. **OQ-03 — When are results durable and mutually consistent?** Must queue and extraction records agree during publication and after an abrupt crash, or only after a completed operation? What recorded state allows unfinished work to resume if the process dies between receiving a model response and saving its result?

   **Production impact:** A crash could lose completed work, leave jobs permanently running or expose a queue entry linked to the wrong extraction version. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Shared operations, Service interruptions and handover; R-61–R-63, R-90–R-91.

4. **OQ-04 — How are outages bounded and retries controlled?** What timeouts, retry limits, backoff and rate-limit behavior apply? Does an unchanged rerun reuse an error or retry it, and does an explicit retry use the failed source/settings or the latest ones?

   **Production impact:** Requests could remain stuck, retries could overwhelm shared model capacity, or recovery could silently process different inputs. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Service interruptions and handover, Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` § Processing and recovery; R-44–R-48, R-63.

5. **OQ-05 — What changes invalidate cached results?** Which prompt, schema, model, configuration, code and policy changes require refresh? Must a routing-only change rerun extraction, and how are affected records discovered and tied to the versions used?

   **Production impact:** A deployment could retain stale routing or trigger unnecessary model calls across the entire intake. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Updates and follow-up, Record and review behavior; R-48, R-58–R-59.

6. **OQ-06 — What constitutes a valid, uniquely identified input?** Does filename identity include a path, and how are duplicate basenames handled? Which export versions and fields are accepted, and what per-document outcome is recorded for malformed JSON, invalid encoding or a missing/non-string message?

   **Production impact:** Unrelated documents could overwrite each other, while malformed exports could disappear from tracking or disrupt a batch. Sources: `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Input export format, Extracted facts, Processing and recovery; R-03–R-06, R-34, R-44.

7. **OQ-07 — What do operators see while work is pending?** During a refresh, is the old result displayed with a stale label, replaced by a pending entry or shown alongside it? Which states and output fields distinguish queued, running, retrying and interrupted work from completed results?

   **Production impact:** Reviewers could mistake stale results for refreshed ones, or operators could fail to locate work that needs recovery. Sources: `CHALLENGE.md` §§ The task, What to submit; `docs/requirements.md` §§ Updates and follow-up, Service interruptions and handover; R-02, R-55, R-61–R-63, R-90–R-91.

8. **OQ-08 — What validation blocks publication?** Beyond JSON/schema validity and provider completion status, which checks must reject impossible dates, empty required values, fabricated quotes or unsupported facts? Should these become extraction errors or null fields with clarification issues, and may malformed model output be repaired automatically?

   **Production impact:** Structurally valid but unusable facts could enter the review queue, or recoverable data issues could cause repeated extraction failures. Sources: `docs/requirements.md` § Record and review behavior; `materials/office-policy.md` §§ Extracted facts, Processing and recovery; `snapshot.schema.json`; R-22–R-28, R-35, R-44, R-64–R-68.

9. **OQ-09 — What reliably triggers instruction-override review?** What distinguishes an override attempt from ordinary access instructions or quoted examples? Must detection inspect the source independently of model-generated issues, and which cases establish adequate detection?

   **Production impact:** An embedded instruction could evade the mandatory inspect-message route, or false positives could overload the service desk. Source: `materials/office-policy.md` § Review queue / rule 1; R-37, R-76.

10. **OQ-10 — What service level must the pipeline sustain?** Are roughly 2,000-message intakes a required supported capacity or sizing context? What completion time, resource/cost limits and maximum delay before completed results become inspectable define acceptable operation under slow or rate-limited service?

    **Production impact:** An implementation could satisfy small sample tests yet accumulate an unmanageable backlog or exhaust resources during an onboarding surge. Source: `docs/requirements.md` §§ Workload and the review day, Verification; R-45–R-46, R-63, R-85–R-86.

from pathlib import Path
import re
p = Path('planning/spec.md')
s = p.read_text()
findings = [
'The requirements mandate the latest processed source and latest-attempt error visibility, but neither the policy nor the supplied exports establishes how concurrent or out-of-order revisions are ordered.',
'The requirements explicitly anticipate overlapping operators and coherent shared records, but leave deployment scope, coordination behavior and duplicate-call prevention unspecified.',
'The requirements demand resumable recorded state and matching queue/extraction versions, but no persistence design defines the durable completion point or crash guarantees, and Python file replacement alone does not establish a transaction across both outputs.',
'The policy requires visible failures, reproducible retries and preservation of earlier successes, but no selected provider or pipeline configuration defines timeouts, backoff, error reuse or which source/settings a retry uses.',
'The requirements establish reuse for unchanged source/settings and refresh with configuration/policy provenance when behavior changes, but do not enumerate cache dependencies or distinguish rerouting from re-extraction.',
'The policy specifies UTF-8 JSON, a message string, filename identity and original-byte hashing, while examples use export version 1.0 and starter checks leave filename collisions, version compatibility and production handling of invalid inputs undefined.',
'The brief requires completed results to remain inspectable and unfinished work to be distinguishable, but defines neither pending-state output fields nor how an older result is displayed during refresh.',
'The policy requires exact quotes, source-supported facts and nulls with issues for uncertainty, while JSON Schema permits empty strings and the supplied schema lacks date constraints, leaving semantic failure classification and automatic repair unspecified.',
'The policy and IT-006 establish inspection routing with evidence for an explicit override attempt, but do not define broader detection criteria, harmless-quotation handling or independent source inspection.',
'The requirements describe 200–400 daily messages and roughly 2,000-message surges with continued access to completed work, but provide no measurable service target, provider quota or capacity evidence beyond the starter sample checks.'
]
parts = re.split(r'(?=^\d+\. \*\*OQ-)', s, flags=re.M)
assert len(parts) == 11
for i, finding in enumerate(findings, 1):
    indent = '    ' if i == 10 else '   '
    parts[i] = parts[i].rstrip() + '\n\n' + indent + '#### Findings\n\n' + indent + finding + '\n\n'
updated = ''.join(parts).rstrip() + '\n'
assert updated.count('#### Findings') == 10
assert updated.split('## Open Questions')[0] == s.split('## Open Questions')[0]
p.write_text(updated)
print('Added 10 one-sentence Findings subsections; requirements unchanged.')
